Mohandas Gandhi. Revered as Mahatma, the Great Soul, he was the spiritual and political leader of India's independence movement against British colonial rule. His philosophy of nonviolent resistance, called satyagraha, transformed anti-colonial struggle, inspired global civil rights movements, and established him as an icon of moral conscience in the twentieth century.

Gandhi developed the philosophy of satyagraha, truth-force, a form of nonviolent civil disobedience that challenged the moral authority of colonial rule without matching Britain's military power. He led the Salt March in 1930, a 240-mile march to the sea to produce salt in defiance of the British salt monopoly. This galvanized mass support and international attention, becoming one of history's most famous acts of civil disobedience. He organized the Quit India Movement in 1942, demanding immediate British departure, which accelerated negotiations leading to independence in 1947.

Gandhi endured repeated imprisonment, beatings, and torture by British authorities, whose violent suppression of his nonviolent protests exposed colonialism's brutality to the world. The Jallianwala Bagh massacre in 1919, where British troops killed hundreds of Indian protesters, crystallized opposition to British rule and vindicated Gandhi's moral authority. He used fasting as a political weapon, using his personal sacrifice to resolve religious communal violence and pressure political rivals, demonstrating an ascetic spiritual authority that transcended mere politics.

Gandhi developed khadi, homespun cloth, as a symbol of Indian self-reliance and independence, turning textile production into a spiritual and political practice that unified the independence movement. His influence extended far beyond India. The American civil rights movement, anti-apartheid activism in South Africa, and peace movements worldwide drew inspiration from his philosophy of moral force. Tragically, Gandhi was assassinated in January 1948 by a Hindu extremist opposed to his communal reconciliation efforts, martyring him at the very moment of Indian independence. His death shocked the world and exemplified the violence his opponents employed against his nonviolent resistance. Gandhi remains connected to India's independence as the movement he led to successful conclusion, the British Empire as the colonial power whose rule he successfully challenged, and the global civil rights movements his philosophy inspired across continents and generations.
